title: Thousands of Messages, One Cable

sections.title: Three senders, one cable
sections.narration: Three cameras want to send data through one cable. Do we need to tell two of them to wait outside? Not always. Let's see how different signals can share a path and still arrive separately.
sections.takeaway: Multiplexing lets independent channels share a physical resource.

sections.title: A medium is not a channel
sections.narration: The cable is the physical medium. The channels are the separate conversations using it. Think of one road with an agreed way to organize the traffic. Sharing a cable doesn't magically add extra wires.
sections.takeaway: One physical medium can carry multiple logical channels.

sections.title: Combine, carry, separate
sections.narration: The multiplexer combines the inputs. The demultiplexer separates them at the other end. Big names, simple jobs: mix with a rule, then use that rule to recover the originals. Random mixing would be a disaster.
sections.takeaway: Sharing works only if the receiving end can separate the streams.

sections.title: Read a frequency picture
sections.narration: Let's give frequency a simple meaning: how many cycles happen each second. Bandwidth is a range of frequencies. Watch us move from waves changing over time to showing where each signal fits on that frequency scale.
sections.takeaway: A frequency plot shows where signal energy is allocated.

sections.title: Give every stream a band
sections.narration: With frequency division, each channel gets its own band. All three can send at the same time. It's more like separate lanes than taking turns. The receiver uses the frequency bands to tell them apart.
sections.takeaway: FDM separates simultaneously active channels in frequency.

sections.title: Leave room between neighbors
sections.narration: These gaps are guard bands. Real filters don't have perfectly sharp edges, so the gaps help keep neighboring channels from interfering. They're useful breathing room, but they also use some of our available spectrum.
sections.takeaway: Guard bands trade usable spectrum for easier channel separation.

sections.title: Filter at the receiver
sections.narration: We want the green signal, so a bandpass filter keeps its frequency range and reduces the others. Imagine choosing one radio station. We're selecting a band, not waiting for the green signal to get a turn.
sections.takeaway: A receiver can extract one frequency allocation with suitable filtering.

sections.title: Work an FDM allocation
sections.narration: Let's do the numbers. Three channels need twenty kilohertz each, with two five-kilohertz gaps between them. Twenty, five, twenty, five, twenty: seventy kilohertz altogether. We're leaving any extra outside margins out of this example.
sections.takeaway: Three 20 kHz channels plus two 5 kHz gaps need 70 kHz.

sections.title: What happens when one is idle?
sections.narration: Now B goes quiet, but its reserved frequency band stays there. A and C don't automatically get to use it. It's a little like an empty reserved seat while everyone else is standing nearby.
sections.takeaway: A fixed allocation can waste capacity when its owner has nothing to send.

sections.title: Now divide the time axis
sections.narration: Let's share by time instead. The cable is still one path, but now the colored blocks take turns using it. Both ends follow the same timing plan, so the receiver knows whose data is arriving.
sections.takeaway: TDM distinguishes channels by when they transmit.

sections.title: Assign repeating time slots
sections.narration: First A, then B, then C. Repeat. That schedule gives each source a turn. Now follow the mixed sequence at the receiver: it gets separated back into the right streams, in the right order.
sections.takeaway: Synchronous TDM gives channels scheduled opportunities to transmit.

sections.title: Understand a TDM frame
sections.narration: One complete A-B-C cycle is a TDM frame here. That word can catch us out: we're talking about a group of time slots, not automatically the same kind of frame used by Ethernet.
bullets: A frame contains one slot cycle
Frame here means a TDM cycle
sections.takeaway: A TDM frame groups the slots in one repeated schedule.

sections.title: Keep the schedule aligned
sections.narration: Both ends need to agree on when each slot starts. Otherwise, B's data could be mistaken for A's. It's like joining a dance one beat late: the steps may be fine, but the timing is wrong.
bullets: Sender and receiver agree on slots
sections.takeaway: Slot timing must be understood at both ends.

sections.title: Work a TDM rate example
sections.narration: Each camera sends two megabits every second. Three cameras need six megabits per second of useful shared capacity. The real link may need more, because keeping the timing organized also takes some extra information.
sections.takeaway: Three continuous 2 Mb/s streams require 6 Mb/s of useful link capacity.

sections.title: The empty-slot problem
sections.narration: B has nothing ready, but its turn still comes around. Meanwhile, A and C may be waiting with data. Fixed time slots are easy to follow, but an empty turn can waste time on a busy link.
sections.takeaway: Fixed TDM can leave a slot idle even when another input has data.

sections.title: Allocate turns on demand
sections.narration: Let's give turns to the sources that actually have data. Here, that's A and C. This is statistical TDM. It saves empty turns, but we need labels or shared information to identify who's sending each part.
bullets: Labels or state identify the source
sections.takeaway: Statistical sharing adapts to demand but needs coordination.

sections.title: Move from copper to fiber
sections.narration: Now let's use light. One fiber can carry several wavelength channels together. The colors help us follow them in the drawing. Watch those channels join the same strand, then reach their separate outputs.
sections.takeaway: Optical fiber supports channels carried on distinct wavelengths.

sections.title: Combine different wavelengths
sections.narration: WDM separates optical channels by wavelength. Think of different light channels travelling side by side, rather than waiting in a queue. The colors are a teaching guide; real fiber systems choose their wavelengths carefully.
sections.takeaway: WDM combines distinct wavelength channels on a fiber.

sections.title: Separate the light again
sections.narration: Combining the light is only half the job. At the receiver, optical components separate the wavelengths again. Each channel needs to get back to the correct output. Sharing is useful when we can undo the mix.
sections.takeaway: An optical demultiplexer separates wavelength channels at the destination.

sections.title: Work a WDM capacity example
sections.narration: Here's another quick total: four wavelength channels, each carrying ten gigabits per second, give forty gigabits per second in raw rate. Useful application data can be lower once the system's extra work is included.
sections.takeaway: Four independent 10 Gb/s channels total 40 Gb/s before overhead.

sections.title: Sharing has physical limits
sections.narration: Sharing a fiber doesn't cancel physics. Signals can weaken, spread, or pick up noise. Multiplexing helps us organize a link's resources. It isn't a cheat code for unlimited data or a perfectly clean signal.
sections.takeaway: Multiplexing organizes existing resources; it does not remove physical constraints.

sections.title: Compare the three schemes
sections.narration: Same sharing problem, three different rules. FDM says, 'Use different frequency bands.' TDM says, 'Take different turns.' WDM says, 'Use different optical wavelengths.' The receiver follows the matching rule to separate the inputs.
sections.takeaway: Ask which dimension separates the channels.

sections.title: Choose with the traffic in mind
sections.narration: Which method wins? That depends on the traffic and equipment. Steady streams may suit fixed allocations. Bursty traffic can benefit from serving whoever has data ready. The best plan fits how the link will actually be used.
sections.takeaway: The useful choice depends on the medium, traffic, and coordination costs.

sections.title: Retell the separation rule
sections.narration: That's multiplexing: several conversations, one physical resource, and a clear way to separate them again. If you remember bands, turns, and wavelengths, you've already got the main picture. The long names can stop looking so scary now.
sections.takeaway: One cable can support several streams when their channels remain distinguishable.
